justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near current price levels and projecting gradual appreciation. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of roughly 255.8 is anchored heavily to the last observed price, with only a small expected move based on typical daily volatility and short-term momentum. At the one-week horizon, the slight increase to 257.2 incorporates a mild positive drift assumption, consistent with a broadly constructive medium-term trend while acknowledging mean-reverting tendencies over short windows. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 259.0 extends that drift further, reflecting a baseline assumption of modest continued appreciation consistent with longer-run trend growth, though the incremental gain per day slows as uncertainty dominates directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 7.3 points is driven primarily by typical daily realized volatility. At one week, the interval expands to roughly plus or minus 14 points, consistent with scaling daily volatility by the square root of time. At one month, the interval balloons to approximately plus or minus 29 points, capturing not just compounded daily noise but also the possibility of regime shifts, macro surprises, or technical breakdowns that become increasingly plausible over longer windows.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a sudden tightening in financial conditions, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions could produce a swift repricing well below the lower bound of the one-month interval. A liquidity event or flash crash, while low probability, could breach even the one-day interval. On the upside, a positive policy surprise such as an unexpected rate cut signal from a central bank, a strong earnings or economic data beat, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above the upper bounds, particularly at the weekly and monthly horizons where there is more time for such catalysts to materialize and compound.

It is also worth noting that these intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes and no structural breaks in the underlying series. If realized volatility were to spike — as it does during risk-off episodes or major data releases — the actual distribution of outcomes would have fatter tails than my stated intervals imply. The intervals are best interpreted as a reasonable baseline under normal market conditions, not as worst-case or stress-scenario bounds.
